title: Big O: how work grows
summary: Feel O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n^2) with workers, boxes, and tiny concrete counts before arrays and windows.

teach.md: **n** is the input size — how many items, or how big the problem is. Work is how many steps the computer takes; Big O names how that work grows as n grows. Explain again opens sticks-and-boxes.

frames.caption: n is on the horizontal axis — input size, not the amount of work.
Steps (how much work) are on the vertical axis. Watch how each family grows as n doubles.
At the same n the four curves sit far apart — steeper ones explode sooner.
You place the sticks. Try O(1), O(n), and O(n²) and watch how many steps change with n.

presentation_raw.md: Two correct solutions can feel totally different as n grows. Before arrays or windows, we need Big O: a shared language for how work grows.

frames.caption: We will watch how counts change as n doubles.

expandable_hint.summary: How work grows as n grows
expandable_hint.md: Point at the four curves: O(1) stays flat, O(log n) rises slowly, O(n) climbs with n, and O(n²) shoots up fastest.

worked_example.md: At n=16, O(1) is still 1, O(n) is 16, and O(n²) is 256. Same n, very different work.

frames.caption: At n = 16 the four families are far apart. O(n) is the middle line.

worked_example_alt.md: Start from the flat line. O(1) barely moves while O(n²) climbs away as n grows.

frames.caption: Same axes: highlight how flat O(1) stays while O(n²) rises.

teach.md: Reading `a[0]` is one array lookup. That work stays 1 even when n grows. That flat work is **O(1)** — Big O names how work grows.

frames.caption: Start here: reading a[0] is one lookup — one unit of work.
As n grows, that lookup count stays 1. The O(1) line stays flat.
Only O(1) on the axes: the line does not move. That flat family is O(1).

probe.prompt_md: Reading `a[0]` takes 1 step when n = 4. About how many steps when n = 1000?

frames.caption: Still reading a[0]. Does a much larger n change the step count?

misconceptions.note_md: That would grow with n. O(1) stays flat — still one lookup.

probe.explain_md:
O(1) does not grow with n.
A longer array does not add lookups for `a[0]`.

explain_frames.caption: Still one lookup at any n.

probe.solution_md: O(1): reading a[0] is one lookup for any n.
probe.hint_md: Does the array get longer, or does the number of lookups change?

probe.prompt_md: Reading `a[0]` takes 1 step when n = 10. About how many steps when n = 10_000?

frames.caption: Still reading a[0]. Does a much larger n change the step count?

misconceptions.note_md: O(1) stays flat. Still one lookup.

probe.explain_md:
Constant work ignores n.
`a[0]` is still one read.

probe.prompt_md: If a constant-time check costs 1 step at n = 2, about how many at n = 64?

frames.caption: Still reading a[0]. Does the step count stay 1?

misconceptions.note_md: Constant means the count does not climb with n.

probe.explain_md:
O(1) is a flat line.
n = 64 does not add steps here.

teach.md: **O(log n)** grows slowly. Each step can cut the space in half. When n doubles, add about one step.

frames.caption: Each curve is labeled at the end. O(log n) is the slow riser.
Bridge: when n doubles, log work usually adds about one step.
Only O(log n): each doubling of n adds about one step.

probe.prompt_md: O(log n) takes 3 steps at n = 8. About how many steps at n = 16?

frames.caption: n doubles once. How many steps now?

misconceptions.note_md: Doubling n adds about one log step (3 → 4), not a double.

probe.explain_md:
Halving 16 needs one more step than 8.
So 3 becomes 4.

explain_frames.caption: One extra halving when n doubles.

probe.solution_md: O(log n): about +1 step when n doubles.
probe.hint_md: When n doubles, log work usually adds one step.

probe.prompt_md: O(log n) takes 2 steps at n = 4. About how many at n = 8?

frames.caption: Another doubling.

misconceptions.note_md: n doubled, but log work adds about one step: 2 → 3.

probe.prompt_md: Binary search style: n goes 16 → 32. About how many extra O(log n) steps?

frames.caption: One doubling.

misconceptions.note_md: Doubling n adds about one log step, not many.

probe.explain_md:
Each doubling adds one halving.
Extra work ≈ 1.

teach.md: **O(n)** grows with n. One full pass visits every item. When n doubles, work about doubles.

frames.caption: Each curve is labeled at the end. O(n) climbs in step with n.
Bridge: one full pass visits every item — work scales with n.
Only O(n): double n, double the work.

probe.prompt_md: A single loop does 8 steps when n = 8. About how many steps when n = 16?

frames.caption: One pass over every item.

misconceptions.note_md: A full pass visits new items too — O(n) doubles when n doubles.
That is closer to O(n²). One pass is O(n).

probe.explain_md:
One visit per element means work ≈ n.
Doubling n roughly doubles steps.
probe.solution_md: O(n): one pass → about n steps.
probe.hint_md: If you visit every item once, how does the count compare to n?

probe.prompt_md: A scan does 4 steps at n = 4. About how many at n = 8?

frames.caption: Linear doubling.

misconceptions.note_md: Linear work grows with n.
One pass is O(n), not n².

probe.explain_md:
Work tracks n.
4 → 8 when n doubles.

probe.prompt_md: One pass over n = 5 items costs about 5 steps. About how many at n = 10?

frames.caption: Another linear check.

misconceptions.note_md: O(n) scales with n.
That would be n² territory.

probe.explain_md:
Linear means roughly n steps.
n = 10 → about 10.

teach.md: **O(n log n)** sits between linear and quadratic. Think: log-cost work for each of n items. Doubling n grows a bit more than 2×.

frames.caption: Each curve is labeled at the end. O(n log n) sits between O(n) and O(n²).
Each curve is labeled at the end. O(n log n) sits between O(n) and O(n²).
Only O(n log n): a bit more than double when n doubles.

probe.prompt_md: At n = 8, an O(n log n) count is 24. About how many at n = 16? Use n · log₂ n.

misconceptions.note_md: Not just 2×. The log factor ticks up: 8·3=24, 16·4=64.
256 is n² at n=16. Here n · log₂ n = 64.

probe.explain_md:
Use n · log₂ n.
16 · 4 = 64.
More than 2×24, less than n².

explain_frames.caption: Faster than n, slower than n².

probe.solution_md: O(n log n) ≈ n · log₂ n → 16 · 4 = 64.

probe.prompt_md: Using n · log₂ n, what is the count at n = 4?

frames.caption: n · log₂ n at n = 4.

misconceptions.note_md: Include the log factor: 4 · 2 = 8.
That is n². We want n · log₂ n = 8.

probe.prompt_md: Using n · log₂ n, what is the count at n = 32?

frames.caption: n · log₂ n at n = 32.

misconceptions.note_md: Include log₂(32) = 5 → 32 · 5 = 160.
n² is bigger. Here 32 · 5 = 160.

teach.md: **O(n²)** grows fast. Nested pair loops do much more work as n grows. When n doubles, work grows about 4×.

frames.caption: Each curve is labeled at the end. O(n²) is the steepest.
Bridge: nested pair loops — when n doubles, work grows about 4×.
Only O(n²): the count explodes as n grows.
Feel O(n²): cross-pair every box with every box and count the sticks.

probe.prompt_md: A pair-check does 64 steps at n = 8. About how many steps at n = 16?

frames.caption: n doubled. What happens to n²?

misconceptions.note_md: n doubled, but n² means about 4× work: 64 → 256.
That undershoots. Quadratic at n=16 is 16² = 256.

probe.explain_md:
8² = 64 and 16² = 256.
Doubling n multiplies quadratic work by about 4.

explain_frames.caption: Quadratic jumps hard when n doubles.

probe.prompt_md: At n = 4, pair-checks do 16 steps. About how many at n = 8?

frames.caption: Quadratic doubling.

misconceptions.note_md: n² grows about 4× when n doubles: 16 → 64.

frames.caption: Square n.

misconceptions.note_md: Square it: 5 · 5 = 25.
n² means n times n.

teach.md: At n=16: O(1)≈1, O(log n)≈4, O(n)≈16, O(n log n)≈64, O(n²)≈256. Later patterns move work down this ladder.

frames.caption: The four families on one plot. O(n log n) sits between O(n) and O(n²).
Bridge: pick which family grows fastest at the same n.
Called out: O(n²) is the steepest line here.

probe.prompt_md: Which family grows fastest as n increases: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), or O(n²)?

frames.caption: Pick the fastest-growing family.

misconceptions.note_md: O(n log n) is quick, but O(n²) still grows faster.
O(n) grows, but O(n²) grows much faster.

probe.explain_md:
Compare the n=16 column.
256 dwarfs 64, 16, 4, and 1.
Quadratic dominates this set.

explain_frames.caption: O(n²) is the steepest climb here.

probe.hint_md: Look at which count is largest at the same n.

probe.prompt_md: At the same n, which is larger: O(n) or O(n²)?

frames.caption: Compare O(n) and O(n²).

misconceptions.note_md: For large n, n² outgrows n.

probe.explain_md:
Same n.
n² climbs faster than n.
probe.hint_md: Which count is bigger at n = 16?

probe.prompt_md: Name the slowest-growing family among O(1), O(n), and O(n²).

frames.caption: Slowest climber.

misconceptions.note_md: O(n) grows; O(1) stays flat.
Quadratic is the fastest here, not the slowest.

probe.explain_md:
Flat beats slow growth.
O(1) is the lowest ladder rung.
